title: The Rash Of Tech Outages Has Shaken Consumer Trust
summary: Tech outages are shaking consumer trust. Learn why speed to market risks leaving consumers to absorb the consequences of rapid innovation.
body_markdown:
### **Consumers Are The Biggest Losers In The Technology Race — We Need To Change That**


Tech companies are moving faster than ever with the promise to make life simpler, better, or easier. But doing that requires constant change, fraught with introducing critical updates, improving features and functionality, and getting “there” before other countries do. The problem? This push to win the race threatens consumers’ trust, finances, and feelings of safety.


[Consumers already report AI agents going rogue](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-nuisances-of-ai-assistants-are-putting-consumer-adoption-at-risk/) : purchasing on their behalf, signing up for memberships, and refusing to disconnect from personal systems when instructed. Then there’s last Friday’s nationwide US air travel ground stop that not only stoked chaotic inconvenience but shook consumers’ trust, as the US Transportation Secretary[chalked it up](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/18/us/sean-duffy-ground-stop-faa-trump.html?unlocked_article_code=1.RlE.mruw.ff-cW7bL04fB&smid=url-share) to rushed systems upgrades, the day after Microsoft’s global outage was the[result of a “fix.”](https://abcnews.com/US/outlook-outage-cause-microsoft-reason-teams-down/story?id=138174626) In just five days, consumers witnessed technology failures across[Spotify, Claude](https://www.reuters.com/business/spotify-down-thousands-users-us-downdetector-shows-2026-09-29/) ,[Workday](https://www.livenowfox.com/news/workday-outage-means-employees-across-thousands-businesses-cant-access-accounts) ,[United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/17/apple-microsoft-faa-jpmorgan-outages.html) ,[Apple, and Marriott](https://apnews.com/article/apple-marriott-technology-outages-ff097d2a0bec767baf38a1bd8eff5829) that disrupted work, banking, payroll systems, and travel (a few times). A[cyberattack on Optimizely](https://www.newsweek.com/cyber-attack-websites-affected-12725863) affected nearly 200 websites. Even the National Security Agency wasn’t safe from disruption. Then the White House[replaced its top cybersecurity official](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/19/us/politics/white-house-cyber-director-departs.html?smid=nytcore-ios-share) .


While business leaders each address outages and other failures from the purview of their respective companies, consumers experience the cumulative consequences of rapid technology changes, *not* isolated incidents. With each additional outage, more stress mounts, which only exacerbates the human toll. Consumers bring those worries to their experiences with the tech around them, especially when it fails.


### How Are Tech Outages Impacting Consumer Trust?


Forrester defines trust as “the high expectation of a positive outcome.” Yet consumers, unfortunately, expect companies to fall short. Nearly[three-quarters of consumers agree](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-october-2026-consumer-pulse-survey/SUS204612) that companies won’t use AI responsibly, while fewer than one in five trust organizations to ensure that AI systems used in critical services are safe and reliable. Recent technology outages turn existing doubts about companies into pessimism about tech progress. An early look at a Forrester’s ConsumerVoices Market Research Online Community poll, still currently in the field, shows a majority of the consumers we polled agreeing that the recent outages occurring over the last week have shaken their trust in the advancement of technology.


How fast can tech advance before consumers feel they’re being asked to absorb the brunt of its risk? Our forthcoming Forrester report (publishing the week of November 30) will examine what companies must do to preserve and regain trust through this period of exceptionally unstable technology change. In the meantime, business leaders must understand that:


- **Speed to market isn’t crowning a winner.** Consumers are overwhelmed by the speed of technology evolution, with[45% of US online adults](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-october-2026-consumer-pulse-survey/SUS204612) becoming more fearful the more they learn about AI technology. Being not first, but also not disruptive, is much better than exposing consumers to risk. The desire to be first to market can undermine your ambitions, because the faster you move, the more corners get cut and the more disruption you cause. Do you really want to lay your shortcomings bare for everyone to see?
- **Consumers won’t stay in their lane if they don’t get info they need.** Tell consumers what’s happening before they have to guess. In the US,[38%](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-october-2026-consumer-pulse-survey/SUS204612) of online adults learn about AI because they can’t escape news coverage about it. People feel like they must become experts in what’s happening, learning about systems that failed, when they don’t receive credible, timely information. Just as the COVID-19 pandemic turned everyone into an armchair epidemiologist, the AI arms race is turning everyday people into incidental software engineers.
- **Mitigating consumer risk requires more than a pit stop** **.** AI is[discovering vulnerabilities](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/18/nx-s1-6044230/concerns-grow-after-spate-of-tech-outages-nationwide) that businesses are rushing to patch, sometimes causing issues in the process. The more that goes wrong, the more people are acutely aware of how delicate our tech infrastructure is. Effective technology management requires thoughtful processes and safeguards to minimize the impact of updates, plus clear communication to stakeholders about potential issues, *before* they arise.
- **Tech companies set the rules to** ***their own* race.** Tech giants are jockeying to achieve more powerful AI, computation, and automation and to better enable autonomous experiences. Some tech leaders have set expectations that consumers should embrace risk as the status quo.[Sam Altman recently said](https://cybernews.com/ai-news/altman-bad-things/) , “We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” But “the world” is not a nebulous body that will painlessly absorb risk that the tech creates. Consumers will. And our research is showing they’re not prepared for how bad things could get.
- **Every outage makes technological progress harder to trust.** Rapid technological evolution forces consumers to navigate new interfaces, understand new infrastructure, and cope alone when systems fail.[Sixty-five percent of US online adults and 69% of UK online adults agree](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-october-2026-consumer-pulse-survey/SUS204612) that “the evolution of AI is outpacing the ability to effectively manage it.”[People believe that technology has the potential to improve their lives](https://www.forrester.com/report/meet-the-new-empowered-consumers-2025/RES189759) , but repeated failures make them question whether companies can manage its advancement responsibly.
